cause: The banned words ('actually', 'leverage', 'elevate', 'transformative', 'unlock') each have legitimate non-sloppy uses that are common in human prose. 'Actually' is a standard emphatic/contrastive adverb; 'leverage' as a noun ('points of leverage') or transitive verb ('leverage technology') is correct domain usage; 'transformative' as a past participle verb ('has transformed') is not the sloppy adjective sense; 'unlock' in headlines or technical descriptions is literal. The rule fires on the word string regardless of grammatical role or meaning.

[business/a16z] (Prohibited word found: "leverage". Rewrite without) In venture capital, we spend lots of time thinking about business models, product market fit, inflection points, network effects, viral coefficients and other points of leverage in a business.

[business/a16z] (Prohibited word found: "transformative". Rewrite w) Jeff has been CEO and remains an active executive chairman of OpenTable, which has transformed the restaurant industry—with 20 thousand restaurants.

cause: Two distinct FP clusters. (1) 'in a world where' is a legitimate historical/technical contrast phrase when not used as a rhetorical opener ('Mainframe-style arrays were designed in a world where a single mainframe...'; Paul Graham literary use; PEP technical contrast). (2) 'In conclusion' / 'in conclusion' is a standard section marker in legal opinions, medical abstracts, academic Q&A, and 19th-century literary prose — not slop in those contexts. 'Now more than ever' fired on a Keats poem. 'It's important to note' is more consistently sloppy but fires on legitimate technical doc signaling (MDN, PEP).

cause: Every sample flags 'hopefully' or 'deceptively'. 'Hopefully' as a sentence adverb ('Hopefully, you find them useful') is standard modern English — the prescriptivist objection to it is itself contested and obsolete. 'Deceptively simple' and 'deceptively casual' are legitimate literary devices meaning 'misleadingly simple/casual' — that is the correct meaning, not skunked usage. 'Acting deceptively' in a legal sample is the literal adverb. None of the 30 samples represent genuinely ambiguous or corrupted usage.

cause: 'In my experience' is a standard epistemic qualifier in Q&A, essay, and professional writing — it signals personal-evidence grounding, not bragging. 'As someone who has' is a standard credential citation ('As someone who has moved from the US...' / 'as someone who has raised children'). The rule conflates legitimate first-person grounding with braggadocio. None of the 28 samples actually boasts about an impressive credential — they are all ordinary experiential anchors.

cause: True positives exist where medical or health claims cite vague authority ('Studies suggest inflammation...', 'studies show that blue light...', 'evidence suggests' for parenting claims). However, 'it is considered' in PEPs and RFCs is legitimate standards-document hedging language expressing community consensus, not fake authority. 'Many believe that... prosperity will not last' is a conversational framing sentence in a finance Q&A, not a pseudoscientific claim. The rule is well-targeted for health/medical content but over-fires on standards documents and opinion framing.

cause: 'Certainly' as an adverb of degree or sentence adverb is standard human English ('Certainly they will learn more', 'Certainly schools should teach', 'Is it much harder... Certainly, but...'). It is not a chat-scaffold word — it appears throughout Paul Graham essays and journalistic prose as a normal emphatic or concessive adverb. The chat-scaffold pattern it is supposed to catch ('Certainly! Here is...') requires an exclamation mark and an imperative follow-on, not a bare adverb in flowing prose.

cause: Two sub-patterns both over-fire. 'empty-scene-transition' catches normal narrative connectives ('It turned out that', 'As is usually the case', 'Then I began to study', 'As the day broke') that are the standard tissue of narrative and analytical prose — not thin filler but structural progression markers. 'deictic-summary' catches rhetorical devices like 'One may still argue' and 'That was the point of' which are legitimate analytical moves. The rule conflates genuine empty transitions with all uses of these constructions regardless of whether they carry meaning.

cause: The rule fires on technical standards documents (RFCs, PEPs) and API reference docs (MDN) where 'value' is a mandatory domain term — protocol fields, Python language semantics, CSS property values. These texts legitimately repeat 'value' and 'context' dozens of times per page because those are the technical concepts being specified. The density signal conflates domain-required repetition with LLM stock abstraction. The rule needs domain exclusions or a word list that does not include 'value' for technical content.
